title: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools

subtopics.heading: Running the command prompt elevated
subtopics.notes:
Some commands modify protected OS state and need administrator privileges. The user must be a member of the Administrators group.

Three ways to launch elevated:
- Search 'cmd', right-click > Run as administrator
- Right-click the command prompt shortcut > Run as administrator
- Ctrl+Shift+Enter shortcut from the start menu search

Getting help inside the prompt:
- help (alone): list available commands
- help <command>: specific help
- <command> /? : same specific help, alternate syntax
subtopics.whyOnExam: Many fix-it commands (chkdsk /f, sfc, format, diskpart) require elevation. If a command silently fails, check whether the shell is elevated.
subtopics.commonTrap: Running chkdsk /f on the boot volume in a normal session. It can't lock the volume in use and will offer to schedule it for the next reboot instead.

subtopics.heading: Navigation: cd, dir
subtopics.notes:
- dir: list files and directories in the current working directory. Add a path to list a different one
- cd (or chdir): change the working directory. cd .. moves up one level
- mkdir / md: create a directory
- rmdir / rd: remove a directory
- robocopy: 'robust copy' with many more options than copy (bandwidth throttling, automatic retry on network outage, etc.)
- copy /v: verifies the copy. /y: suppresses overwrite prompt (useful in batch / scripts)

Drive letters: each partition gets a letter. Windows boot drive is usually C:. Use a backslash separator: C:\Users\Professor\Documents
subtopics.whyOnExam: Know what cd .., the /y flag, and the difference between robocopy and copy do. Robocopy is the right tool for unreliable network copies.
subtopics.commonTrap: Forgetting /y in scripted copy commands. An overwrite prompt will hang an unattended script.

subtopics.heading: Disk management commands
subtopics.notes:
chkdsk - Check Disk
- chkdsk: read-only check of the file system index
- chkdsk /f: fix file system errors (requires elevation)
- chkdsk /r: locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implies /f, takes much longer)
- If the volume is in use, chkdsk offers to run at next reboot

format
- Formats a partition with a specified file system. Default if not specified: FAT32
- Example: format K: /FS:NTFS
- ERASES the partition. Always verify the target before running
- Requires administrator

diskpart
- Disk partitioning utility. Starts its own command shell
- list disk / list volume / list partition shows storage layout
- Can create, delete, format, extend partitions
- Requires administrator (UAC prompts if not elevated when launched)
subtopics.whyOnExam: chkdsk /f vs /r is a classic exam target. /f fixes file system errors; /r adds bad-sector recovery.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking format without specifying /FS:NTFS, then being surprised it formatted as FAT32 (the default).

subtopics.heading: Network commands
subtopics.notes:
ipconfig - IP / DNS / DHCP configuration for each adapter. ipconfig /all gives MAC, DHCP server, lease, DNS suffixes

ping - reachability test using ICMP echo. Reports response time and TTL. Default sends 4 echo requests on Windows

netstat - active TCP / UDP connections
- netstat -a: ALL connections including listening ports
- netstat -b: shows the executable for each connection (requires elevation)
- netstat -n: numeric output (no DNS lookups)

nslookup - manually query DNS. Returns the IP(s) for a name, or vice versa

net use - map a network share to a drive letter:
  net use H: \\server\share
net view \\server - lists shares on a server
net user <name> /domain - account details for a domain user

tracert - traceroute. Uses ICMP TTL Exceeded to discover routers between you and the destination. TTL is a hop count, not seconds

pathping - traceroute + per-hop ping statistics. First builds the route, then runs round-trip tests against each hop. Long but useful for identifying which hop is degrading performance
subtopics.whyOnExam: Match the symptom to the right tool: 'is this server reachable?' = ping. 'where in the path is the problem?' = tracert or pathping. 'who is connected to my machine?' = netstat.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming TTL is a time value. In IPv4 traceroute, TTL is a HOP COUNT - it decrements at each router.

subtopics.heading: File management commands
subtopics.notes:
- md / mkdir: make a new directory
- rd / rmdir: remove a directory
- copy: copy a file. /v verifies, /y suppresses overwrite prompt
- robocopy: 'robust copy'. Throttling, automatic retry on network outage, supports very large copies. /? shows pages of options
subtopics.whyOnExam: robocopy is the right answer for large or unreliable network copies. copy is fine for local single files.
subtopics.commonTrap: Using copy where robocopy belongs. A single dropped packet during copy = corrupt destination. Robocopy retries automatically.

subtopics.heading: Informational + OS management commands
subtopics.notes:
Informational
- hostname: name of the current device. Use it to confirm you're on the right machine before destructive actions
- whoami: who you're logged in as. whoami /all adds SID, group membership, privileges
- winver: opens a dialog with the Windows version, build, and edition
- net user <name>: account info (locked, last logon, expires, groups, etc.)
- <command> /?: built-in help for that command

OS management
- gpupdate /force: re-apply group policy to this device immediately (instead of waiting for the next refresh)
- gpresult /r: report which group policies are currently applied (RSoP = Resultant Set of Policies)
- sfc /scannow: System File Checker. Scans protected Windows files and repairs any that were modified or corrupted. Log saved to cbs.log
subtopics.whyOnExam: hostname + whoami are your sanity checks before issuing a destructive command remotely. sfc /scannow is the standard 'something replaced my Windows files' fix.
subtopics.commonTrap: Running gpupdate without /force. Without /force, only changed policies refresh; with /force, every policy reapplies (slower but thorough).
